q: In networking, the word "node" means:
o: Only the main server of the network
The cable that joins two computers
Any device connected to the network, such as a computer or printer
x: A node is any device attached to a network that can send, receive or pass on data: a computer, printer, switch and so on. A server is one kind of node, not the only one.

q: The physical arrangement in which the computers, cables and other devices of a network are connected is called the network's:
x: Topology is the layout of the connections, such as bus, star, ring or mesh. A protocol is the set of rules for communication, not the layout.

q: A network made by joining two or more different topologies, for example several star networks linked to one bus cable, has which topology?
x: Combining different topologies in one network gives a hybrid topology. A pure bus would have every computer tapped onto the one cable, without the star parts.

q: What is the main reason for joining the computers of an office into a network?
o: To share resources such as files, printers and an Internet connection
To make each computer's processor run faster
To increase the RAM in every computer
To stop computers from needing an operating system
x: Networking lets users share data, printers and an Internet connection and communicate with each other. It does not change a single computer's processor speed or RAM.

q: In a star network, the central switch stops working. What is the effect?
o: Only the computer nearest to the switch is affected
None of the computers can communicate through the network
The computers pass data around in a ring instead
Nothing changes, because each computer has its own cable
x: In a star, all data between computers passes through the central device, so if it fails the whole network stops. Each computer having its own cable only protects the others when one cable, not the centre, fails.

q: In a bus network, why does performance usually drop as more computers are added?
o: All computers share one cable, so there are more collisions and waiting
Each new computer needs its own cable to a central switch
Data has to pass through every computer in a loop
The terminators stop working when more computers join
x: Every computer on a bus uses the same backbone cable, so with more computers more transmissions clash and have to be resent. Passing data through every computer in a loop describes a ring, not a bus.

q: A client-server network has only one server, which holds all the shared files. What happens if this server fails?
o: The clients start sharing files peer-to-peer automatically
The clients cannot reach the shared files and services
Nothing, because each client keeps a copy of the server's files
x: In a client-server network, the shared files and services live on the server, so its failure cuts the clients off from them. Clients do not automatically turn into a peer-to-peer network.

q: Compared with a WAN, a LAN usually has:
o: Higher data rates and fewer errors over a smaller area
Lower data rates and more errors over a larger area
The same speed, but it always uses satellites
A larger area, because it uses telephone lines
x: A LAN covers a building or campus with its own short cables, so it is fast and reliable. A WAN covers great distances over leased or public links, which are usually slower and costlier.

q: A WAN that joins offices in different countries usually carries data over:
o: One short coaxial cable in a single building
A single hub in the head office
Leased telecom lines, undersea cables and satellite links
x: Distant sites are linked through telecom providers' long-distance lines, cables and satellites. Infrared only works over a few metres in line of sight, so it cannot join offices in different countries.

q: A client-server network grows from 10 clients to 200 clients that all send their requests to the same single server. What problem is most likely?
o: The clients can no longer send requests at all
Each client must now act as a server
The server becomes a bottleneck and responses slow down
The network changes into a ring topology
x: Every request goes to the one server, so as the number of clients grows it has more work than it can handle quickly. The clients can still send requests; they simply wait longer for replies.

q: Which pair correctly matches a network with its type?
o: Computers in one school building: WAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: LAN
Computers in one school building: MAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: LAN
Computers in one school building: WAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: MAN
Computers in one school building: LAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: WAN
x: One building is a small area, so it is a LAN; branches across the country cover a very large area, so they form a WAN. A MAN covers about one city, which is too large for one building and too small for a whole country.

q: Four friends share files in a peer-to-peer network. Sara switches her computer off. What happens?
o: The whole network stops, because Sara's computer was the server
Files kept only on Sara's computer cannot be reached; the others still share
Nothing changes, because the files are stored on a central server
All the other computers are switched off automatically
x: In peer-to-peer each computer shares its own resources, so only what is stored on Sara's computer becomes unavailable. There is no central server in peer-to-peer, so the others carry on.

q: A full mesh network has 6 computers. A seventh computer is added and the network is kept a full mesh. How many new links are needed?
x: The new computer must have its own link to each of the 6 existing computers, so 6 links are added (the total goes from 15 to 21). 21 is the new total, not the number of new links.

q: Six computers P1 to P6 form a ring in which data travels only in the direction P1 → P2 → P3 → P4 → P5 → P6 → P1. P2 sends a message to P1. Through how many other computers does it pass on the way?
x: Going one way only, the message goes P2 → P3 → P4 → P5 → P6 → P1, so it passes through P3, P4, P5 and P6: 4 computers. P1 is next to P2, but only in the opposite direction, which this ring does not use.

q: Two star networks each have 5 computers, every computer joined by its own cable to that network's switch. The two switches are then joined by one cable. How many cables are used in total?
x: Each star needs 5 cables, giving 5 + 5 = 10, and one more cable joins the two switches: 10 + 1 = 11. 10 forgets the cable between the switches.

q: Which OSI layer is closest to the user and is where protocols such as HTTP and FTP work for programs like browsers?
x: The Application layer is the top layer (layer 7), giving network services to user programs through protocols such as HTTP, FTP and SMTP. The Physical layer is at the bottom, dealing with raw bits on the medium.

q: In the term "IP address", what does IP stand for?
x: IP is the Internet Protocol, which gives each device a logical address and carries packets across networks. A company that sells Internet connections is an Internet Service Provider, not IP.

q: What does FTP stand for?
x: FTP is the File Transfer Protocol, a standard set of rules for copying files between computers over a network. The other expansions are not real protocol names.

q: Counting from layer 1 upward, which list gives the first four OSI layers in the correct order?
x: Layer 1 is Physical, layer 2 Data Link, layer 3 Network and layer 4 Transport, followed by Session, Presentation and Application. Swapping Network and Transport puts end-to-end delivery below routing, which is wrong.

q: In the TCP/IP suite, which protocol gives each packet its source and destination addresses and routes it across networks?
x: IP handles logical addressing and routing of packets between networks. TCP works above it, making delivery reliable and in order, but it does not route packets.

q: Which protocol does an e-mail program commonly use to download received messages from the mail server to the user's computer?
x: POP3 (Post Office Protocol 3) collects incoming mail from the server to the client. SMTP is used to send mail towards a server, not to download received messages.

q: Which of the following is written in the form of an IPv6 address?
x: IPv6 addresses are written as groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, with :: standing for a run of zero groups. 192.168.10.1 is an IPv4 address, and www.example.pk is a domain name.

q: Each of the four numbers in a dotted-decimal IPv4 address can have which range of values?
x: Each number is one octet of 8 bits, and 8 bits give values from 0 to 2⁸ − 1 = 255. So 256 or 300 can never appear in an IPv4 address.

q: The IPv4 address 127.0.0.1 (the loopback address) is used to:
o: Refer to the computer itself, for testing its own network software
Reach the main DNS server of the Internet
Send a message to every computer on the LAN
Connect directly to the ISP's router
x: Packets sent to 127.0.0.1 never leave the computer; they loop back to it, which is useful for testing. A message to every computer on a LAN uses a broadcast address, not the loopback address.

q: In the IPv4 address 192.168.1.10, the last octet 10 is written in 8-bit binary as:
x: 10 = 8 + 2, so the bits for 8 and 2 are 1: 00001010. 00010000 is 16, which comes from reading "10" as if it were hexadecimal.

q: At the sending computer, each OSI layer adds its own control information (a header) to the data it gets from the layer above. This is called:
x: Wrapping the data with each layer's header on the way down is encapsulation; the receiver removes the headers on the way up. Encryption scrambles data for secrecy, which is a different job.

q: Which pair correctly matches an OSI layer with the name of its data unit?
x: The Network layer handles packets, the Data Link layer frames, the Transport layer segments, and the Physical layer raw bits. Frame and segment are swapped in two of the wrong pairs.

q: A network uses the subnet mask 255.255.255.192. How many addresses in each subnet can be given to hosts?
x: 192 = 11000000, so the mask leaves 6 bits for hosts: 2⁶ = 64 addresses, minus the network address and the broadcast address, gives 62. 64 forgets to remove those two addresses.

q: With the subnet mask 255.255.255.0, which address is on the same network as 192.168.4.17?
x: The mask 255.255.255.0 means the first three numbers name the network, so the network is 192.168.4; only 192.168.4.200 shares it. 192.168.40.17 looks similar, but its third number is 40, not 4.

q: Which pair correctly matches two protocols with the OSI layers at which they work?
o: HTTP: Session layer; TCP: Network layer
HTTP: Application layer; TCP: Transport layer
IP: Transport layer; TCP: Application layer
IP: Data Link layer; HTTP: Transport layer
x: HTTP serves user programs at the Application layer, TCP gives end-to-end reliable delivery at the Transport layer, and IP routes packets at the Network layer. Putting TCP at the Network layer confuses it with IP.

q: What does NIC stand for in networking?
x: A NIC is a Network Interface Card, the hardware that connects a computer to a network. Each NIC has its own MAC address.

q: Which device connects two networks that use different protocols, translating between them?
x: A gateway converts data from one protocol to another so that dissimilar networks can communicate. A repeater only boosts signals, and a hub only copies them to all ports.

q: Where is a computer's MAC address normally stored?
o: In the DNS server of the Internet
In the router's list of websites
In its network interface card, set by the maker
x: The MAC address is a physical address built into the NIC during manufacture. The IP address, not the MAC address, is the one a network or DNS deals with.

q: A router decides where to send each arriving packet by looking up the destination address in its:
o: List of MAC addresses on one port
x: A router keeps a routing table of networks and the best next hop to reach each one. A list of MAC addresses per port is what a switch keeps, not a router.

q: In a busy LAN, the central hub is replaced by a switch. What is the usual result?
o: More traffic, because a switch copies frames to every port
No change, because hubs and switches work in the same way
Less unwanted traffic, because frames go only to the destination port
The LAN must start using IP addresses instead of cables
x: A switch reads destination MAC addresses and sends each frame only to the right port, so other computers are not loaded with traffic. Copying frames to every port is how a hub works.

q: At the receiving end of a telephone-line connection, a modem changes the analogue signal back into digital data. This step is called:
x: Turning the received analogue signal back into digital data is demodulation, the 'dem' part of modem. Modulation is the opposite step, done at the sending end.

q: A switch has 24 ports. One port is used to connect it to the router, and every computer uses one port. At most, how many computers can be connected to this switch?
x: One of the 24 ports is taken by the router link, leaving 24 − 1 = 23 ports for computers. 24 would leave no port for the router.

q: In a star network of 6 computers with a hub at the centre, computer P sends a message to computer Q. Which computers receive the signal?
o: Only Q, because the hub reads Q's MAC address
Only P and Q, because the others are switched off by the hub
All the other five computers, but only Q keeps the message
None, because a hub cannot forward any data
x: A hub works at the Physical layer and copies every signal out of all its other ports, so all five receive it; the NICs of the other four see it is not for them and ignore it. Sending only to Q is what a switch does.

q: Which list puts a hub, a switch and a router in order of the OSI layer at which each mainly works, lowest layer first?
x: A hub works at layer 1 (Physical), a switch at layer 2 (Data Link, using MAC addresses) and a router at layer 3 (Network, using IP addresses). Putting the router before the switch reverses layers 2 and 3.

q: In data communication, the path along which the message travels from the sender to the receiver, such as a cable or radio waves, is called the:
x: The medium is the physical path the signal travels through, wired or wireless. The protocol is the set of rules both sides follow, not the path itself.

q: Which statement describes an analogue signal?
o: It varies smoothly and continuously over a range of values
It has only the two values 0 and 1
It can only be sent through fibre-optic cable
It is made of separate start and stop bits
x: An analogue signal is a continuous wave, like the sound of a voice, that can take any value in a range. A signal with only separate values such as 0 and 1 is digital.

q: Which wireless technology is commonly used to connect a mobile phone to wireless earphones a few metres away?
x: Bluetooth uses short-range radio waves to link nearby devices such as phones and earphones. Satellite and microwave links are for long distances, and coaxial cable is not wireless at all.

q: In which modulation is the frequency of the carrier wave changed according to the data, while its amplitude stays the same?
x: Frequency modulation changes how often the carrier wave repeats, keeping its height constant. In amplitude modulation it is the height that changes and the frequency stays the same.

q: Data is sent as one continuous block of characters, and the sender and receiver are kept in step by timing signals, with no start and stop bits around each character. This is:
x: In synchronous transmission both sides share timing, so blocks of data flow without start and stop bits for each character. Asynchronous transmission is the kind that frames every character with a start bit and a stop bit.

q: Sending all 8 bits of a byte at the same time over 8 separate wires is called:
x: In parallel transmission several bits travel side by side on separate lines at once. Serial transmission sends the bits one after another along a single line.

q: In a wave diagram of a signal, the height of the wave from its middle line to its peak is called its:
x: Amplitude is the size or strength of the wave, measured as the height of a peak. Frequency is how many cycles occur each second, which is shown by how close together the waves are, not their height.

q: Which is an important advantage of fibre-optic cable over twisted-pair copper cable?
o: It carries much more data over longer distances
It is cheaper and easier to join
It carries electricity to power the computers
It can bend around very sharp corners without loss
x: Light pulses in glass fibre give very high bandwidth and lose little strength over long distances. Fibre is actually more expensive and harder to join than copper, which is its main drawback.

q: Which list contains only guided (wired) transmission media?
o: Twisted-pair cable, coaxial cable, fibre-optic cable
x: Guided media send signals along a physical path, which is true of twisted-pair, coaxial and fibre-optic cables. Microwave, infrared, radio, satellite and Bluetooth travel through air or space, so they are unguided.

q: Which of the following is naturally an analogue signal?
o: The bits sent from a keyboard to the computer
The data stored in a byte of RAM
The changing voltage from a microphone as a person speaks
The on/off pulses in a USB cable
x: A microphone produces a voltage that rises and falls smoothly with the sound wave, which is analogue. Keyboard codes, RAM bytes and USB pulses are made of separate 0 and 1 values, so they are digital.

q: Which pair correctly matches each example with its transmission mode?
o: Radio broadcast: half-duplex; video call: simplex
Radio broadcast: full-duplex; video call: half-duplex
Radio broadcast: simplex; video call: full-duplex
Radio broadcast: simplex; video call: half-duplex
x: A radio station only sends and listeners only receive, which is simplex; in a video call both people speak and hear at the same time, which is full-duplex. Half-duplex would force the callers to take turns, like a walkie-talkie.

q: Why is synchronous transmission more efficient than asynchronous transmission for sending a large file?
o: It sends each character separately, so no timing is needed
It does not add start and stop bits to every character, so fewer extra bits are sent
It uses analogue signals, which carry more bits than digital ones
It adds a start and a stop bit to every character, which checks each one
x: Asynchronous transmission adds at least 2 extra bits to each 8-bit character, while synchronous sends whole blocks with only a little control information. Adding start and stop bits to every character describes asynchronous transmission, the less efficient one.

q: HTML is the:
o: Language used to create and structure web pages
Protocol that sends e-mail between servers
Address of a website's home page
x: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses tags to mark up the headings, text, images and links of a web page. Sending e-mail between servers is the job of SMTP, not HTML.

q: Bilal sends an e-mail and adds his CV as a PDF file that travels with the message. The PDF file is called an:
x: A file sent along with an e-mail message is an attachment. The inbox is the folder where received messages are kept.

q: A private network inside a company, built with Internet technologies such as web pages but open only to the company's own staff, is called an:
x: An intranet uses the same tools as the Internet (browsers, web pages, e-mail) but only for the organisation's members. The Internet is the public worldwide network open to everyone.

q: A website address ending in .edu is generally used by:
x: The .edu domain is used for educational institutions such as universities and colleges. Government sites use .gov and commercial companies typically use .com.

q: To return later to a useful web page without remembering or retyping its address, you can save it in the browser as a:
x: A bookmark (called a favourite in some browsers) stores a page's address so it can be opened again with one click. A cookie is a small file a website stores to remember the user, not something the user saves to revisit a page.

q: Using Boolean search operators, which pages match the query `cricket OR hockey`?
o: Only pages containing both cricket and hockey
Pages containing cricket, hockey or both
Pages containing cricket but not hockey
x: OR widens the search: a page matches if it contains at least one of the words. Requiring both words is what AND does.

q: A search engine can show results in a fraction of a second mainly because it:
o: Visits every website on the Internet at the moment you search
Asks each website's owner to send matching pages
Stores only the pages that you visited before
Searches its own index of pages collected earlier by crawler programs
x: Crawler (spider) programs visit pages ahead of time, and the search engine builds an index of their words; a search looks up that index. Visiting every website at the moment of searching would take far too long.

q: Which of the following is a correctly formed e-mail address?
x: An e-mail address has a user name, then one @ sign, then the mail domain, with no spaces. The address with a space is invalid, and the others either lack the @ or have nothing before it.

q: Which statement about the Internet and the World Wide Web is correct?
o: The Web is one service that runs on the Internet; e-mail and FTP are other Internet services
The Internet and the Web are two names for exactly the same thing
The Internet is one service that runs on the Web, like e-mail
The Web is the cables and routers, and the Internet is the web pages
x: The Internet is the worldwide network of networks; the Web is the system of linked pages that uses it through HTTP, alongside services like e-mail and FTP. Treating the two words as the same thing is the common mistake.
